claims.text: The target material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
Conventional arc melting of the target alloy typically introduces trace oxygen and nitrogen impurities.
Vacuum induction or plasma arc melting under a highly purified inert atmosphere can minimize oxygen and nitrogen pickup relative to standard arc melting.
Ultra-high-purity processing will reduce interstitial oxygen and nitrogen concentrations in the alloy matrix and at grain boundaries.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen can promote phase segregation during high-temperature aging.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen impurities will suppress impurity-induced phase segregation.
Reducing interstitial impurities will produce a more uniform atomic distribution.
Reducing interstitial impurities will suppress nanoscale phase-segregation zones identified as PFZs.
Interstitial impurities act as nucleation sites for unwanted phase segregation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Impurity-promoted segregation depletes strengthening interstitial solutes from the metal matrix.
Depletion of solute interstitials from the matrix during aging causes progressive mechanical softening.
Eliminating interstitial impurities will preserve or enhance solid-solution strengthening by maintaining uniform solute distribution.
The ultra-high-purity processed alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield or compressive strength than the conventionally arc-melted control.
The proposed comparison applies to elevated-temperature tensile or compression testing of a single-phase Ti- and Ni-primary alloy.

The magnitude of any strength improvement is uncertain because baseline impurity concentrations and distributions are not quantified and cooling-rate or heat-treatment differences may introduce variability.
